You likely haven't heard of "Cimarron Strip," and that's just fine. "Cimarron Strip" was a short-lived Western series that aired on CBS for 23 episodes in 1967 and 1968. Unlike most shows of the day, it was a 90-minute program that followed the struggles of Marshal Jim Crown (Stuart Whitman), who has been placed in quite an awkward position. "Cimarron Strip" takes place in 1880 on a contested strip of land between the then-border of Kansas and the First Nations people's land. The local Kansan settlers are waiting for the government to grant them title to their land, and Jim Crown has arrived to tell them that Washington won't do that and that their leases have all been revoked.  Naturally, this sparks a wave of violent resentment from the local cattlemen, and Jim Crown finds he is the only marshal in town, and that the army has abandoned him. Historically, the strip of land in question would eventually become the Oklahoma panhandle, and was notoriously ungoverned for about a decade. "Cimarron Strip" was wise to set a series in this place and time. The show's cast was rounded out by Jill Downsend, who plays a young woman named Ducley who arrives on the Cimarron Strip to learn that her father has died, and meets her father's old business partner, a Scot named MacGregor, who let their inn go to pot. The show also included the ambitious Francis Wilde (Randy Boone), an aspiring reporter and photographer.  Although "Cimarron Strip" was short-lived, it was but a drop in the bucket for Stuart Whitman, who has hundreds of credits to his name. He worked constantly from his first screen credit in 1951 through his retirement in 2000.  Stuart Whitman was so prolific that it's likely you've seen multiple of his movies and TV shows without even trying. He got his start playing uncredited bit parts in the sci-fi classics "When Worlds Collide" and "The Day the Earth Stood Still," and swiftly moved into the Western circuit, appearing on TV shows like "The Roy Rogers Show" and "The Range Rider." He was in the backgrounds of a dozen movies before getting steady credited work by the mid-1950s.  Stuart Whitman was in 13 episodes of "Highway Patrol," and landed his first leading role in 1957 in the movie "Johnny Trouble." The late 1950s saw a renewed explosion of opportunities for Whitman, and his film roles are plentiful. In 1961, he played the main character in Guy Green's "The Mark," for which Whitman was nominated for Best Actor at the Academy Awards. Whitman was thereafter in "The Longest Day," and starred in multiple TV shows and movies every year. He had one of those soulful, hangdog faces that made him instantly sympathetic but was also dedicated to his roles, often projecting a natural confidence that casting directors love. I recall first seeing him in "Night of the Lepus" in 1972, a silly horror movie about giant killer rabbits. There was nothing Stuart Whitman wouldn't do.  I could list all of Stuart Whitman's credits here, but it would just take up a lot of time. Children of the 1990s might know him as Jonathan Kent from the "Superboy" TV series, from his guest spots on "Knots Landing," the pilot for "The Adventures of Brisco County, Jr.," or the voice of Mule Morgan on "Aaahh!!! Real Monsters." Stuart Whitman has a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, and it's quite earned. I have always had a great deal of respect for the hard-working actors in Hollywood who only sometimes lead projects, but who serve as reliable, pliable professionals who always stand beside the lead. Supporting players and character actors like Stuart Whitman keep the entire industry standing.  Stuart Whitman's last credit came in 2000, when he appeared in the Chuck Norris-starring TV movie "The President's Man." After that, Whitman seemingly retired, living the last 20 years of his life away from the cameras. Whitman died of skin cancer in 2020 at the age of 92. The industry lost a minor legend. According to IMDb, Whitman had 191 credits. He is notable for the volume of his output alone.  As for "Cimarron Strip," it was an ambitious project that might have been Whitman's longest-running TV gig. TV vet Vincent McEveety directed several episodes, and the notoriously litigious Harlan Ellison wrote one. Joseph Cotton, Leslie Nielsen, Robert Duvall, Michael J. Pollard, Elisha Cook, David Carradine, John Saxon, Darrin McGavin, and John Voight all have guest roles on the series. The Harlan Ellison episode is about the potential return of Jack the Ripper.  One can watch 16 episodes of "Cimarron Strip" on the streaming service Fawsome, although it seems no service has all 23 episodes lined up. One has to find the out-of-print DVD box set for that, which can be purchased on the second-hand market.

While tech companies are pouring billions into AI infrastructure, they are also competing fiercely for AI talent — and the AI boom is reshaping the choices available to workers. Alongside established giants like Apple, Google, and Amazon, frontier AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic now offer the chance to work at the edge of a technological shift, with potentially significant financial upside. Meanwhile, years of tech layoffs have made job security a bigger consideration for many workers. We asked eight tech workers about their dream employer, the Big Tech companies they're most and least interested in, and whether they've pursued jobs at OpenAI or Anthropic. (Their responses have been edited for length and clarity.) Abhinav Bohra is a senior applied scientist at Amazon. He's in his 30s and lives in Seattle. Have you tried to land a job at an AI lab like OpenAI or Anthropic? A couple of recruiters for AI labs have reached out to me, including one at another Big Tech company. I took the calls but never pursued them. Labs hire people to make models smarter. I build recommendation engines, and a frontier lab has no real use for one yet: no catalog, no sellers, no shoppers to rank for. The day one of them runs an actual marketplace, people like me get very interested in them. We're not there yet. Between Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and NVIDIA, which company would you most (or least) want to work for? Amazon, which is boring, so here's the runner-up: NVIDIA. Recommendation at scale has become an inference cost problem. Running a big model once is cheap. Running it for every search and every shopper in real time is where the money goes. When your unit of progress is the millisecond, NVIDIA sits upstream of everything. Create a BI Job Scout and get opportunities matched to your goals. Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.                                      Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                    Each company could be a good fit for someone in my field, but I also imagine they all have teams I'd love and teams I'd dread. Mike Kostersitz is a senior director, product management at Nike. He's in his early 60s and lives in Oregon. If you could work for any tech company, what would it be? If I had to look outside Nike, Anthropic would be my dream employer. The pull is real, and the company's stated values align more closely with my own than some other companies. The original Tamagotchi was a plastic egg about 50 mm tall that you clipped to your bag and tried not to kill. Thirty years later, Bandai has announced a version you wear on your finger, the 39th entry in the main series, and by far the smallest one yet. The Tamagotchi Ring houses a 0.56-inch color LCD in a body 28 mm tall, roughly half the size of that 1996 keychain, and it took Bandai two years to figure out how to make it work. Miniaturizing something this far doesn’t happen by shrinking the parts. It requires rethinking the entire internal layout. The Tamagotchi Ring contains 64 total components, 52 electronic and 12 plastic, crammed into a body measuring 28mm x 23mm x 35mm. The 0.56-inch display is the smallest color LCD ever fitted to a Tamagotchi, and the battery, now rechargeable rather than a replaceable coin cell, charges via an included case because there simply wasn’t room for anything else. The design sits on the finger like a small wearable sculpture rather than a piece of consumer electronics. The Tamagotchi has been through enough reinventions to know when a milestone deserves something genuinely new rather than a color variant. A ring-form virtual pet is a different object than a keychain pet, even if the creature inside behaves the same way. It changes where the Tamagotchi lives in your day and how visibly you’re tending to it. Bandai hasn’t announced plans for a direct international launch, so international buyers are looking at third-party import channels for now. Fifty thousand vintage cameras and lenses sit inside a Finnish warehouse, and most of them arrived broken. A collection that size raises a simple question: how do you find anything worth shooting with, and does the vault actually hold the one lens you have been chasing for years? That hunt drives a two-day tour that Mathieu Stern takes through Camera Store, a company based in Tampere that repairs and resells old gear. Stern first visited six years ago when the operation was small, and returning for its 10-year anniversary means walking through a place with roughly 15,000 items listed online and another 30,000 in some stage of checking and repair. His guide, listing manager Connor, opens what he calls the treasure trove, a room stacked with screw-mount Leicas and rows of M2 and M3 bodies waiting for hands that know how to bring them back. Some repairs take days. The whole system runs on codes, where a body gets pulled from the warehouse by number and matched to a technician who knows that specific fault. The finds get stranger as the tour moves. Stern handles an Agfa 35mm TLR, a twin-lens design almost never made in that format, along with a Kodak Medalist II that has no comfortable way to hold it and an Ihagee Exakta that counts as one of the first widely popular SLRs. There is a Nikon L35 AW AF built to survive shallow water, a pair of Linhof Technorama 617 panoramic cameras that eat 120 film, and a transparent Ricoh FF-9 special edition. Connor pulls a Leica post camera used decades ago by telephone offices to photograph their call ledgers, then a Nikon 8mm fisheye with filters built into a rear ring because nothing fits on that bulging front element. A Hasselblad XPan, sold by Fuji as the TX-1, gets its moment, as does a Pentax 67 with the 105mm f/2.4 and its wooden grip. The prices climb fast in a few spots. Three copies of the Canon 50mm f/0.95 sit in one place, and Connor guesses the stack in his hands runs near 10,000 euros before deciding not to think about it. Stern's personal target turns out to be a Canon 85mm f/1.2 aspherical in Canon FD mount, cleaned and running close to new. Between those, the tour keeps landing on cheap oddities: the Konica Tomato, the yellow Minolta Weathermatic, and the Olympus μ II, which sells for around 550 euros and refuses to stay in stock. Connor's own favorite point-and-shoot is the Konica Big Mini, one of the smallest 35mm cameras ever made. The pull of these cameras tracks a shift that has been building for years. Film prices and darkroom talk get most of the attention, but the demand Connor describes points somewhere broader: people buying old point-and-shoots and camcorders to record moments without a phone in the loop. The Olympus μ II going for the price of a used mirrorless body is not nostalgia alone. A whole generation grew up with every photo living inside a glowing rectangle, and a fixed-lens 35mm camera forces a different pace, one frame at a time with no screen to check. If you have a drawer of gear you stopped using, that same demand works in your favor. The market Connor works in treats a scuffed 110 camera and a five-figure Leica lens as parts of the same catalog, which means the thing gathering dust at home has a value you can actually look up. Watch the full vault tour in the video above to see which cameras Stern walks away wanting and how deep the collection really goes. Alex Cooke is a Cleveland-based photographer and meteorologist. He teaches music and enjoys time with horses and his rescue dogs.

Back in 2023, HP released the Envy Move, an all-in-one (AIO) PC with a clever quirk: It could run wirelessly on battery power. The average lifespan was around 4 hours, but it was enough to watch a movie, join a video call, or have a playful family interaction with its touchscreen on whatever app or website you wanted. To make it even more portable, HP included a built-in handle attached to a flexible loop on its top side, pop-out feet on its underside, and a rear pouch that held a keyboard with an included touchpad. It was genius; a 24-inch touchscreen PC with great speakers that moved wherever you needed it. Its design could have used some tweaks, but its downsides didn't feel at all severe, resulting in a perfect score in my Envy Move review. It was the most remarkable sample I'd ever tested, but it quickly became evident that consumers weren't interested enough to choose it over a traditional laptop or desktop.      Following my review in 2023, the Envy Move was later discontinued from HP's official storefront and third-party retailers across the world, while the broader Envy range itself was dropped alongside the Spectre, Pavilion, and Dragonfly names, in favor of a major HP portfolio overhaul that introduced 'Omni' and 'Elite' PCs to replace them. HP all-in-ones now sit alongside higher-end models like the impressive OmniStudio X, but nothing replaced the Envy Move, leaving any remaining stock with its already modest Core i7-1355U mobile processor from Intel's 13th generation. It was never intended to be a high-performance machine, but I'm sure modern, efficiency-centric Intel chips would have supercharged it perfectly. Then again, if previous-generation components could maintain the ~$900 price tag on an Envy Move with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage, I'd let it slide. Frankly, I doubt many customers in HP's target audience would care to scrutinize its specific choice of processor, especially when the experience is great nonetheless, but future models could have been even better.      In the following summer, HP's Envy Move made a few appearances at my family gatherings and various parties, watching UEFA Euro 2024 matches in a shaded garden during BBQs in the best weather. At one point, I even connected an old Guitar Hero controller to its built-in Bluetooth receiver and turned it into a type of arcade machine; it was so much fun. Everyone who would listen was impressed by what I could demonstrate, but nobody was particularly interested in replacing their long-lasting laptops or self-built desktop PCs. Its appeal should have been clear; anyone looking to share a family PC with their children would surely love its touchscreen and a general theme of collaboration, but it still fizzled out. It's just the way she goes. Sometimes, brands take a risk and let something unusual escape the concept phase, but it never comes with a guarantee that enough people will buy it. I've seen plenty of oddities at conventions like CES, but they usually come with the understanding that it's just brands flexing their manufacturing muscles, showing what they could do if they wanted to. The Envy Move felt different, but it ultimately doesn't matter how much I admired it, at least not compared to the sales figures that PCs need to pull in to stand a chance. Instead, I just keep my fingers crossed that it could make a comeback someday, or that the people who helped the Envy Move earn a Good Design award would at least know how much I admired what they made. To be clear, the only reason I suddenly felt all nostalgic and bubbly about an AIO PC is that I started seeing bizarre knockoffs popping up on TikTok and Instagram Reels. Strange, Android-based screens lampooning the same kind of unique selling point as the Envy Move, pulling in frustratingly positive comments about how good the idea is — I know it's a good idea. Laptops are great, and custom-built desktop PCs are even more rewarding when you can afford it, but all-in-one PCs still have their place. HP tried something unique with the Envy Move, and it's something I'll still praise in the hopes that it tries again when the timing is right (if that ever happens). Let's see what turns up at CES in 2027.      Join us on Reddit at r/WindowsCentral to share your insights and discuss our latest news, reviews, and more. The age of all-electric Volkswagen California camper van life is finally here. VW was definitely way too late to the party to launch the first electric camper van, and we can't even say it developed the cutest. But it does finally have an official all-electric California camper van on the way to market. In fact, the all-new ID. California Cruise is even closer than expected, with deliveries slated to begin next year. And it's priced cheaper than any existing model in the midsize California camper van family.  As Volkswagen mentioned in teasing the ID. California Cruise concept, the new member of the California family isn't merely the automaker's first all-electric camper van but the "first member of a new all-electric California family," a lineup Volkswagen plans to grow out over the next two years.  As the first launch in that e-camping lineup, the California Cruise is quite simple and straightforward, a sleeper van without a kitchen, toilet or in-vehicle dining area. It doesn't include a pop-up roof option, either, instead limiting overnight accommodations to just two people. The folding bed stacks in the tailgate area for travel and unfurls atop the folded rear seats, delivering a sleeping area of 203 x 120 cm (80 x 47 in) atop a cushy, newly developed 9-cm (3.5-in) mattress. The package skips any form of standard or optional kitchen unit but does include a full set of blackout blinds and ventilation grilles for the front windows meant to increase airflow and cut out condensation when sleeping inside. Those buyers that specify a panoramic glass roof will also get a blackout blind for the entire roof, letting them better block out unwanted early-morning sun or brightly blazing full-moon light.  Volkswagen rounds out the camper kit with a table set that includes two folding chairs, making the ID. California Cruise essentially a high-spec ID. Buzz with Good Night Package – not exactly an overly compelling way to kick off the official VW electric camper van era but a safe one with little downside. And in that case, the actual "Good Night" kit might find better use as a retrofit for existing owners who decide they want a camper van option later down the line.  As compared to the Ququq kit-equipped ID. Buzz camper van we tested out two years ago, the ID. Cruise's sleeping and camping amenities appear more neatly integrated into the base van itself, without the need to install a separate box. On the downside, the factory camper van lacks the fridge, sink system and cooking equipment that Ququq integrates into its all-in-one camper system.  The ID. California Cruise benefits from a new "California" mode that incorporates a new control unit for operating lighting and comfort features while camping. Much like on the recently updated California PHEV camper van, this feature also lets campers use traction battery power for heating or cooling the interior during overnight camping stays. In the case of the California Cruise, it supports stationary heating or air conditioning for up to 48 hours per stay, depending on battery level and outdoor temperatures. In effect, the little California Cruise becomes a fully climate controlled tiny RV.  Campers can also tap into battery power at base camp via the California Cruise's vehicle-to-load capability. They can plug everything from coffeemakers and electric cookers to ebike chargers and outdoor lighting systems into the vehicle and power them with up to 2,000 watts continuous/3,600 watts peak output, no need to lug around a large standalone power station.  Volkswagen has also updated the California app with a charging station tracker that displays charging stations along the planned route. The idea is that owners can plan the entire trip, including specific charging stops along the way. Once at the station, the Plug & Charge feature of the Volkswagen app starts the charging immediately and automatically once the cable is connected, no need to enter any additional info. This feature is supported at select charging stations.  The ID. California Cruise is built atop the ID. Buzz Pro on buyer's choice of short or long wheelbase. It starts at a price of €60,791 (approx. US$70,400), quite comparable to what an identically equipped ID. Buzz Pro with Good Night package would cost. The surprising bit is that Volkswagen's first all-electric camper van costs €5,295 less than the lowest priced member of the midsize California camper van family: the €66,086 ($76,525) California Beach.  The Beach's pop-up roof and slightly larger size can easily explain that price difference, but the fact that the ID. California Cruise sleeps the same two people in a comparably comfortable fashion really erases the usual premium that electric vehicles command, making the California Cruise a nice value for buyers who want an electric everyday driver and an on-demand camper van for casual overnighting.  It's also worth noting that the ID. California Cruise is close to the European equivalent of the Tourer 4Motion camper van Volkswagen already announced for the US market. However, the US-market camper is only available as a long-wheelbase van with 4Motion all-wheel drive, so it remains to be seen if it prices near or north of that $70,400 equivalent.  Volkswagen will begin the first ID. California Cruise deliveries in early 2027. It plans to add additional all-electric California camper van models by 2028, so perhaps a pop-top and/or fully equipped camper with kitchen will arrive in the near future. Lawrence Shankland's second-half penalty at Aberdeen earned Derek McInnes his first Scottish Premiership win as Rangers boss Highlights: Aberdeen v Rangers 30/08/26 Until Sunday's trip north to Aberdeen, Derek McInnes had not really enjoyed watching his Rangers team. There had been flashes of fun in the dugout for the Ibrox boss, but a run of two wins in seven matches meant his dream job was in danger of spiralling out of control. Having overseen European elimination before the end of August, McInnes led his players to Pittodrie, where he once spent eight years as manager, with pressure intensifying around his future. However, despite delivering another unconvincing display, the Rangers manager believes the hard-fought Scottish Premiership win, earned by Lawrence Shankland's second-half penalty, can lay the foundations for a successful tenure. "Contrasting feelings from Thursday night," McInnes said. "It was a tough few days for us all. I thought today we were far more like the Rangers team I want us to be. "Probably for the first time this season, I really, really enjoyed watching the team. "There have been moments of enjoyment, a couple of wins and some passages of play, but we know when we come here that you can't be sparkling for 90 minutes. "You need to compete and bring quality, and I thought we did all that." There are "no monetisations in this game". Rockstar has confirmed Grand Theft Auto 6 will launch without microtransactions or generative AI. The confirmation came during a group conversation with Kinda Funny Games ahead of the GTA 6: Extended Look, where Kinda Funny's Andy Cortez asked whether players would be able to spend real money on in-game purchases. Rockstar said there are "no monetisations in this game", and Greg Miller followed up, asking "point-blank" whether generative AI had been used anywhere in GTA 6's development. Rockstar told him there's "no AI" in the game, either (thanks, IGN). Earlier this year, Take-Two Interactive, the parent company of GTA developer Rockstar Games, reportedly laid off its AI team, including its head of AI. Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick has previously plainly stated that AI is incapable of creativity of its own, but it was his strongest message yet that Take-Two's approach to AI bucks an industry trend that has seen more and more studios pivot to AI tools, most recently at the cost of human translators and human-made in-game artwork. Zelnick is very much an outlier, though. Many other game companies, including Krafton, Square Enix, EA, and more, have invested heavily in the new tech. There will, however, be gated content in GTA 6's Ultimate Edition. Priced at £90 – £20 above the £70 standard edition – it bundles in exclusive cosmetics, vehicles, weapons and even a handful of shops and services unavailable to standard edition owners, including the Electric Fang tattoo parlour and Stock 305 clothing store. Rockstar's own support page confirms standard edition owners will be able to buy the Ultimate Edition upgrade separately after redeeming their copy, with the bonus content "threaded across all aspects of Jason and Lucia's story" and unlocked chapter by chapter. Grand Theft Auto 6 is due out on 19th November for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S. This week's GTA 6 bonanza revealed a wealth of new information about the game, such as a changed Wanted system, a changed carjacking system, a new romance system, a huge game world, and a list of in-game activities. This is what a billion dollars gets you, observed Chris Donlan, though as Chris Tapsell pointed out, this push towards realism and away from easy-going fun is a huge risk for the series – even if, he argued, it's ultimately right that it takes it. Undervolting is a straightforward approach to lowering your PC's operating temperature, and it can be applied to both the CPU and the GPU. Over my many months of experimenting with undervolting, I've tried a few variations of this approach, including undervolting the CPU to stabilize throughput, undervolting and overclocking my GPU at the same time, and of course, setting a custom fan curve while undervolting that delivers the best balance between performance and temps. Recently, I decided to experiment again with undervolting on my Ryzen 5 7600X, and this time, I noticed an additional effect that I didn't quite associate with undervolting at all, adding to its expanding list of benefits. Here's what I found, and why it's relevant for those who rely extensively on single-core performance in productivity tasks and gaming.  Across almost all of my undervolting experiments, if there's one thing I can confirm, it's the fact that the Ryzen 7000-series Zen 4 processors respond exceptionally well to undervolting. This tendency seems to be a pattern for the SKUs, as previously, TechPowerUp similarly noted that it helps the chips to hold higher boost multipliers more consistently. I've experimented with a -15 Curve Optimizer offset on my Ryzen 5 7600X before, but after trying different settings over time, I found that my particular chip responds better to -11, which is what I use generally by applying a negative 11 offset across all cores. Of course, due to silicon variance, this isn't a recommendation for every 7600X, and stability testing is still the gold standard to gauge if a particular offset is right for a chip. Ryzen Master utility makes it incredibly easy, too. All one needs to do is select the Curve Optimizer, switch it to an all-core negative offset, enter the desired value, and save it as a profile. The only catch with this method, though, is that it is session-only and after a reboot, these settings have to be applied again. That's something that is well-intended, since an unstable undervolt can potentially result in a crash loop, and it guards against that occurrence. Undervolting is easier and more beneficial than ever   Most users will ever explore undervolting because of the thermal benefits, and that's entirely fair. Speaking frankly, that was my sole expectation going into this run as well, but I did observe an anomaly (positive, of course) that was worth talking about. There's no news when it comes to thermal improvement. The peak CPU temperatures dropped from 80°C to 68°C, while power consumption fell from roughly 104W to 94W. What instead caught my attention was that performance went up ever-so-slightly alongside it. Across the runs on Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, which happens to be heavily CPU-bound, the average frame rate went up from roughly 81.3 FPS to 83.3 FPS, which is a modest 2.5% improvement over baseline. Even more interestingly, I capped the display resolution to 1080p despite running a 1440p-capable display so that MSFS 2024 would be main thread limited, rather than GPU-limited. However, I wouldn't confidently attribute the entire performance margin to the Curve Optimizer offset alone. Flight Simulator has a considerable run-to-run variance, to the point that even my two stock runs differed by around 5 FPS despite identical settings. In hindsight, however, what I can say with more confidence is that the CPU sustained a higher clock while consuming less power and producing less heat, which is characteristic of undervolting.  Perhaps what's more interesting is how the chip responded to undervolting. With the -11 offset applied, the 7600X's average clock went up from 5.40GHz to 5.45GHz, despite CPU power dropping by around 10W. Average CPU temperatures also fell by 12°C, while peak temperature was around 17°C lower. This seems to suggest that the undervolt gave the CPU a considerably more efficient operating point. Instead of spending more power as well as thermal headroom to maintain the boost clock, the chip here was able to sustain a slightly higher clock while operating within a lower power and temperature envelope. The GPU also saw an increase in utilization alongside this. While all interesting observations in their own right, what I did not expect was for the CPU to clock higher after undervolting. The usual expectation with undervolting is that you exchange performance for lower temps and power consumption, but that does not seem to be the trade-off here. To the contrary, the 7600X reached a slightly higher reported clock while drawing less power and with less heat output. You can't just lower the voltage and expect your desired results Undervolting will not make every CPU faster, and my results here certainly aren't enough to make that claim. What they have shown, time and again, is that lowering voltage does not automatically imply you would be giving up on performance under every condition either. On my 7600X, the Curve Optimizer offset delivered what it promised, and also allowed the chip to reach a slightly higher clock. It's also worth remembering that every chip responds to undervolting rather uniquely, and so, with the same offset, it's possible that your SKU may deliver better and more consistent performance. In any case, it's worth experimenting with. We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful. Most camping gear exists in one of two categories: either it’s practical and ugly, or it looks great and makes you sacrifice half your trunk space to bring it along. Portable fire pits have historically landed in the second camp. They fold, sure, but “fold” usually means collapsing from one large, awkward shape into a slightly less large, slightly more annoying one. The RTE FireFold from Rough Trails Equipment has a fundamentally different idea about what “portable” should actually mean. The FireFold earned its name honestly. Collapsed, it packs down to just 1.8 inches thick, the kind of flat that slides directly into the same sleeve where you’d carry a laptop. It debuted at Overland Expo Mountain West and reportedly stopped people mid-stride, which makes complete sense. A fire pit you’d walk past without recognizing isn’t exactly something the outdoor gear industry has offered before. Designer: Rough Trails Equipment       Performance numbers don’t suffer for the sake of the profile. The FireFold runs on liquid propane and delivers 320,000 BTU per hour, which is a genuinely serious output for something that stores like a piece of tech hardware. Setup takes seconds. The adjustable regulator gives you real control over the flame, not just the on-or-off binary you get from plenty of other portable options. It ships with a ripstop storage bag, the kind of small-but-telling detail that signals the designers were thinking about actual use patterns rather than just the product photo.  What makes the FireFold worth talking about beyond its specs is what it communicates about design priorities. Rough Trails Equipment built this specifically for overlanders and van-lifers, a community that has spent years quietly making peace with compromise. Amazon has pushed a key change to the use of DRM on its Kindle platform that has users up in arms. And the timing couldn't be any worse, with an unknown change to the way popular ebook library app Libby works also causing uproar in the Kindle community. And both changes have the potential to push Kindle owners towards alternatives like Kobo. Neither of the changes was officially announced, and both were spotted by Kindle users first. But they both impact the way a ton of Kindle owners use their eReader in ways that shouldn't be downplayed. The most infamous Kindle deletion solved the wrong digital ownership problem  The first change relates to Amazon's Kindle Digital Rights Management, or DRM. Earlier this month, it was noticed that a new Kindle Oasis software update made it harder to download ebooks from the device. Software version 5.18.2.1.1 was pushed out without any release notes to detail what changes it included. But we now know that it hardens the DRM that protects ebooks stored on Kindles. We now know that Kindle Oasis devices running software version 5.18.2.1.1 are now impervious to most DRM-removal tools. And this isn't an isolated incident. Amazon rolled out the same upgraded encryption across its device lineup starting in 2025. Older 10th-gen Kindles and the Paperwhite 4 lost jailbreak support earlier in 2026, and the first five generations of Kindle were cut off from having their ebooks downloaded in May of this year. The Oasis lineup was one of the last major holdouts. Now, the Kindle Voyage appears to be the only model that hasn't received a software update to add the new, tougher DRM. And it's surely only a matter of time before it does.  Arguably the bigger issue for some people is a new change that impacts users of the Libby library app. Libby allows readers to borrow ebooks from public libraries via the OverDrive system. Books borrowed from the Libby app can be loaded onto a Kindle, and they are automatically removed when the loan expires. But that removal only happens if the Kindle has an internet connection. As you've probably already figured out, Kindle users have long used that fact as a way to extend their loan period. Putting a Kindle into Airplane Mode prevented Libby from revoking an ebook's license, allowing the reader extra time. The next time the Kindle connected to the internet, the license would be removed. It's important to remember that using the Airplane Mode trick didn't prevent anyone else from borrowing the same ebook. As far as Libby was concerned, the license was revoked. It handed the ebook to the next person in line without issue. A victimless crime, if you will. However, since mid-August we've seen Reddit threads aplenty confirming that the Airplane Mode trick no longer works on newer Kindle hardware. The Kindle Paperwhite 11th- and 12th-gen models are included, as is the Colorsoft Signature Edition. Users say they are prompted to re-enable Wi-Fi before the expired ebook will open. Once they do, it's game over. Oddly, neither Amazon nor OverDrive has confirmed that they made the change that did this — presumably because they know the news won't be well received. Amazon says it hasn't changed anything on its side. But, clearly, something's afoot. Amazon once had the eReader market sewn up, but that's no longer the case. This move has the potential to push some Kindle owners away from Amazon's platform and towards Kobo. It's a shift many people have already considered, and some have already jumped ship. But, ultimately, switching from Kindle to Kobo isn't the win-win that some would have you believe. While it's true that Kobo's DRM is generally easier to remove than Amazon's newly hardened version, that's only part of the story here. There's bad news for anyone switching to Kobo because of the Libby situation. In short, it's pointless: The Airplane Mode trick already doesn't work on Kobo devices. The move to Kobo really is only about the added DRM flexibility that Amazon is in the process of removing from its Kindles.  Individually, either of the changes made to the way people use their Kindles would have been an inconvenience. But together, they feel like more of a targeted push than a coincidence. It's easy to read these changes as Amazon's intent to make sure people don't move their Kindle books to other platforms, locking them in for good. The move also ensures that fewer people can read books on Kindle platforms for free. By removing the Libby loan period workaround, Amazon knows that more people will run out of time. And when they do, there's a chance they'll just buy the ebook via the Kindle Store just to finish it. Whether any of this was Amazon's explicit goal or just a side effect of its tightening of security doesn't really matter. The result is still the same — Kindle readers have less flexibility than they once did. Reading eBooks and taking notes has never been simpler thanks to the Kobo Libra Colour, an innovation upon the classic e-Ink smart notebook that offers 32GB of storage and a full-color display. This notebook is easy to take on-the-go thanks to its IPX8 full waterproof protection, ergonomic controls, and small, portable display — but it's as well-suited for an evening of reading at home. Most people think wealth takes either luck or a side hustle. But the wealthiest Americans know a secret: you don't need a second paycheck if your money is working harder than you are. When you have substantial capital, strategic placements — from real estate to equity stakes — generate enough cash flow to sustain (and grow) a lifestyle without touching a day job. And unlike sweat equity, these vehicles compound quietly in the background, turning initial investments into generational wealth. Keep Learning: What Billionaires' Kids Learn About Money That Few Others Do Act Now: Start Growing Your Net Worth With Smarter Tracking We reached out to Chad Cummings, a certified public accountant (CPA) and attorney at Cummings & Cummings Law who works with the ultra-wealthy, for a breakdown of the four asset classes that consistently make this possible. According to Cummings, real estate is the entry point most commonly used by the upper-middle class to reach high net-worth status. “When held long-term, [real estate] appreciates while tenants service the debt,” Cummings told MoneyLion. As an example, he pointed to a client who bought a duplex in 2011 for $180,000. Today, the property is worth more than $500,000, and the mortgage has almost been paid off. His client “signs one property management agreement per year and does nothing else,” Cummings said. “The [rental] direct deposits hit every month without him lifting a finger.” Stock market investing isn't exclusive to the wealthy. More than 60% of Americans polled by Gallup have some kind of stock market investments. But high earners control the vast majority of stock market wealth and reap most of its benefits. The top 10% of households by net worth control more than 87% of all corporate equity and mutual fund shares, according to Federal Reserve data cited by The Street. When the market surges — like it has for the past three-plus years — that concentration of ownership means these individuals pocket the vast majority of gains. No second income needed.  Private companies represent one of the most underrated wealth-building vehicles available to high earners, Cummings said.  One of his clients invested in a pest control company, and the valuation ballooned from $400,000 to $2.2 million in four years.  "The business itself is the wealth-building vehicle — not the paycheck it generates," Cummings explained. "As a bonus, this creates an asset that can be used as collateral to fund the acquisition of other businesses."  Angel investors are high net-worth individuals who fund startup companies with personal capital. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) sets specific requirements to qualify, and the barrier to entry is intentionally high.  In short, you need to be a high earner to even become an angel investor. Once you reach that status, the risks can be substantial — but so can the rewards. “While risky, angel investments let clients place $25,000 into a pre-revenue startup and either lose it all or see a 75x return,” Cummings said.  “One client wrote a $10,000 check into a SaaS company in 2019 that sold in 2025. His gain exceeded $3 million. The catch: He also lost his entire investment on the next four deals, totaling about $400k, but still came out far ahead on the whole. Most people cannot stomach that loss pattern.” Notice what these four asset classes have in common: they're not income plays, they're capital plays. Real estate, equities, private companies and startups all follow the same blueprint — deploy capital strategically, collect the returns and let compound growth work in the background. That's the real wealth-building system. Ten years ago, if someone said people would still be buying AM4 CPUs in 2026, they'd be laughed at. After all, AMD originally planned to support AM4 only through 2020, but the platform surpassed everybody's expectations, probably even AMD's. Despite AM5's launch in 2022, AMD kept releasing new AM4 CPUs, and now, a decade later, the company has brought one of AM4's most beloved CPUs back to market. There's a reason why people loved the 5800X3D so much. When AM4 was on its last legs, it gave users one final drop-in upgrade. I know how good of an upgrade it was because I went from a Ryzen 9 5900X to the 5800X3D myself before eventually moving to AM5. Back when it launched, it was the best gaming CPU you could buy, but re-releasing it in 2026 is just AMD giving those who missed the boat a second chance. Except this time, I'd argue anyone still considering this CPU is four years too late. Did they accidentally make AM4 too good? Credit where it's due, the 5800X3D was a no-brainer for gamers when it launched in 2022. AMD's 3D V-Cache made a huge difference in cache-sensitive games. It was fast enough to trade blows with Intel's flagship 12900K in gaming benchmarks, all while costing less and not forcing you to buy a new motherboard. If you were already on AM4, a BIOS update was all you needed for this drop-in upgrade. Even if you were upgrading from a 5800X or a 5900X, the 5800X3D was good enough to give you a noticeable FPS uplift. In fact, that's why I sidegraded from the 5900X to the 5800X3D despite giving up four cores. Fast-forward to today, and you have much faster CPUs to choose from. Yes, the 5800X3D still holds its own against newer CPUs, and I wouldn't tell anyone who already owns one to upgrade just yet. But buying one today is a completely different story. Those who upgraded when it first launched already got years of use out of it, but right now, you're paying full price for a CPU that's already two generations behind. My problem with the 5800X3D today isn't the CPU itself. It's the platform you're putting another $349 into. Even though it's a whole $100 cheaper than what early adopters paid in 2022, you're still spending hundreds on a platform that has had nothing new to offer in years. Today, you can get the 7800X3D, which is actually about 20% faster than the 5800X3D, for less. As of this writing, I saw it on Newegg for just $300. Of course, that means paying hundreds of dollars for a new motherboard and RAM kit, but hear me out. If you get a four-year-old CPU like the 5800X3D today, what are the chances you'll stick with it for another four or five years? Sooner or later, it won't be able to keep up with newer GPUs, and then you'll have no choice but to pay for a new motherboard and DDR5 memory anyway. So you're not really avoiding the cost of upgrading to AM5. You're just delaying it while dropping another $349 into AM4 along the way. With AMD planning to support AM5 through 2029, you're better off making the move as soon as possible rather than waiting until it's nearing the end of its life too. Before you come at me in the comments, I'm not writing off the 5800X3D. This CPU can still handle almost any game you throw at it, and at higher resolutions like 1440p or 4K, you're far more likely to be GPU-limited anyway. There are exceptions, like pairing it with an RTX 4090 or 5090, as I did, or playing CPU-bound competitive titles at very high frame rates. But the average gamer won't find the 5800X3D bottlenecking their GPU anytime soon. But there's a big difference between the 5800X3D being good enough to keep and being good enough to pay $349 for in 2026. Buying one today is like buying a PS5 in 2026, knowing it'll be left behind sooner rather than later. Sure, you're avoiding absurd RAM prices today by spending that $349, but nobody knows if or when those prices will come back down. And if you wait another couple of years to make the jump, AM5 won't be as enticing because you may not have a meaningful drop-in upgrade left.
